# List of World Heritage Sites in Arab states

The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) designates World Heritage Sites of outstanding universal value to cultural or natural heritage which have been nominated by signatories to the 1972 UNESCO World Heritage Convention. Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). Natural features (consisting of physical and biological formations), geological and physiographical formations (including habitats of threatened species of animals and plants), and natural sites which are important from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty, are defined as natural heritage.
The Arab States are a region defined by UNESCO. It consists of Arab nations which have accepted the World Heritage Convention, making their historical sites eligible for inclusion on the list as World Heritage sites.  the following nations are listed as Arab States: the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, which signed the convention on 24 June, 1974; Kingdom of Bahrain, which signed the convention on 28 May, 1991; the Arab Republic of Egypt, which signed the convention on 7 February, 1974; the Republic of Iraq, which signed the convention on  5 March, 1974; Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, which signed the convention on 5 May, 1975; the State of Kuwait, which signed the convention on 6 June, 2002; the Republic of Lebanon, which signed on the convention on 3 February, 1983; State of Libya, which signed the convention on 13 October,  the Islamic Republic of Mauritania, the Sultanate of Oman, the State of Qatar, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the State of Palestine, the Republic of the Sudan, the Syrian Arab Republic, the Republic of Yemen, the Republic of Tunisia, and the United Arab Emirates. Countries which have served on the World Heritage Committee include
World Heritage Sites
UNESCO lists sites under ten criteria; each entry must meet at least one of the criteria. Criteria i through vi are cultural, and vii through x are natural.

! scope="row" | Qal'at Bani Hammad
|
| AlgeriaM'sila Province,
| Cultural:AlgDje(iii)
|
| align="center" | 1980
| In a mountainous site of extraordinary beauty, the ruins of the first capital of the Hammadid emirs, founded in 1007 and demolished in 1152, provide an authentic picture of a fortified Muslim city. The mosque, whose prayer room has 13 aisles with eight bays, is one of the largest in Algeria. Beni Hammad Fort is near the town of Maadid (aka Maadhid), about 225 kilometres (140 mi) southeast of Algiers.
|-
! scope="row" | Djémila
|
| AlgeriaSétif Province,
| Cultural:AlgDje(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 1982
| Djémila (formerly known as Cuicul) was a Roman town in a mountainous site, comprising a forum, temples, basilicas, triumphal arches and religious buildings and other structures, each adapted to a location 900 m (3,000 ft) above sea level.
|-
! scope="row" | Casbah of Algiers
|
| AlgeriaAlgiers Province,
| Cultural:AlgKas(ii)(v)
|
| align="center" | 1982
| The Casbah of Algiers is a unique Islamic city on the Mediterranean coast. It contains remains of a citadel, medieval mosques, and Ottoman palaces.
|-
! scope="row" | M'zab
|
| AlgeriaGhardaïa Province,
| Cultural:AlgMzb(ii)(iii)(v)
|
| align="center" | 1982
| The intact, traditional human habitat was built around five ksour of the M'zab Valley in the 10th century by the Ibadites.
|-
! scope="row" | Tassili n'Ajjer
|
| AlgeriaIllizi and Tamanrasset Provinces,
| Mixed:AlgTas(i)(iii)(vii)(viii)
|
| align="center" | 1982
| A vast plateau on the edge of the Sahara, Tassili n'Ajjer contains more than 15,000 cave engravings that record climatic changes, animal migrations, and the evolution of human life, dating from 6,000 BCE to the first centuries CE. It is also noted for its eroded sandstone landforms.
|-
! scope="row" | Timgad
|
| AlgeriaBatna Province,
| Cultural:AlgTim(ii)(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 1982
| Established by Emperor Trajan in 100 CE as a military colony, Timgad features cardo and decumanus streets, constituting a typical example of Roman town-planning.
|-
! scope="row" | Tipaza
|
| AlgeriaTipaza Province,
| Cultural:AlgTip(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 1982
| Previously a Carthaginian trading centre, Tipaza was conquered by the Romans and converted into a military base. The site also bears witness to Paleo-Christian and Byzantine influences.
|-
! scope="row" | Dilmun Burial Mounds
|
| BahrainNorthern Governorate,
| Cultural:BahDil(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2019
| Located in the western part of Bahrain Island, Dilmun Burial Mounds date back to the Dilmun, the Umm al-Nar culture. They were built between 2050 and 1750 BCE include 21 archaeological sites with more than 11 K burial mounds and 17 royal mounds built as 2-storeyed funeral towers.
|-
! scope="row" | Qal'at al-Bahrain
|
| BahrainNorthern Governorate,
| Cultural:BahQal(ii)(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2005
| Qal'at al-Bahrain was the capital of the Dilmun civilization and a place of consistent human settlement and occupation from  to the present. A Portuguese fort stands atop the site.
|-
! scope="row" | Bahrain Pearling Trail
|
| Bahrain
| Cultural:BahPea(iii)
|
| align="center" | 2012
| Consisting of buildings in Muharraq, oyster beds, a segment of the coast, and a fortress, the site testifies to the pearling tradition that dominated the Persian Gulf from the 2nd century to the early 20th century, when the introduction of cultured pearls from Japan resulted in the crash of pearling economy in Bahrain.
|- style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Abu Mena
|
| EgyptAlexandria Governorate,
| Cultural:EgyAbu(iv)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| The ruins of the former Christian holy city contain a church, a baptistery, basilicas, public buildings, streets, monasteries, houses, and workshops, and were built over the tomb of Menas of Alexandria.
|-
! scope="row" | Thebes
|
| EgyptLuxor Governorate,
| Cultural:EgyAnc(i)(iii)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| The former capital of Egypt and the city of Amun, Thebes contains temples and palaces at Karnak and Luxor, as well as the necropolises at the Valley of the Kings and the Valley of the Queens, bearing witness to the height of the Egyptian civilization.
|-
! scope="row" | Islamic Cairo
|
| EgyptCairo Governorate,
| Cultural:EgyHis(i)(v)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| One of the world's oldest Islamic cities and in the middle of urban Cairo, the site dates from the 10th century and peaked during the 14th century. Islamic Cairo contains mosques, madrasas, hammams, and fountains.
|-
! scope="row" | Giza pyramid complex
|
| EgyptGiza Governorate,
| Cultural:EgyHis(i)(v)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| Having served as the capital of the Old Kingdom of Egypt, Giza is host to a variety of funerary monuments, including tombs, ornate mastabas, temples, and pyramids.
|-
! scope="row" | International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia
|
| EgyptAswan Governorate,
| Cultural:EgyNub(i)(iii)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| Located along the Nile, the site contains monuments such as the Temple of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel and the Sanctuary of Isis at Philae, saved from being submerged by Lake Nasser as a result of the construction of the Aswan Dam.
|-
! scope="row" | Saint Catherine's Monastery
|
| EgyptSouth Sinai Governorate,
| Cultural:EgySai(i)(iii)(iv)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 2002
| The orthodox monastery of Saint Catherine is among the oldest Christian monasteries still in function. Dating from the 6th century, it is positioned near Mount Horeb where, according to the Old Testament, Moses received the Tablets of the Law. The region is sacred for Christians, Muslims and Jews.
|-
! scope="row" | Wadi al Hitan
|
| EgyptFaiyum Governorate,
| Natural:EgyWad(viii)
|
| align="center" | 2005
| Located in western Egypt, Wadi Al-Hitan contains fossil remains of the now extinct Archaeoceti, mapping the evolution of the whales from a land-based to an aquatic mammal.
|-
! scope="row" |  Ahwar of Southern Iraq
|
| Dhi Qar Governorate, Basra Governorate, Maysan Governorate , and Muthanna Governorate; Irq
| Mixed:IrqAhw(iii)(v)(ix)(x)
|
| align="center" | 2016
| Located in southern Iraq, the site contains three cities of Sumerian origin, namely Uruk, Ur and Eridu, in addition to four wetland areas in the Mesopotamian Marshlands.
|-
! scope="row" | Babylon
|
| IraqBabylon Governorate,
| Cultural:IrqBab(iii)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 2019
| Situated 85 km south of Baghdad, the property includes the ruins of the city which, between 626 and 539 BCE, was the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. It includes villages and agricultural areas surrounding the ancient city.
|-
! scope="row" | Citadel of Erbil
|
| IrqErbil Governorate,
| Cultural:IrqErb(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2014
| Situated on the top of a tell and overlooking the city of Erbil, the Erbil Citadel
corresponds to ancient Arbela, an important Assyrian political and religious centre dating back to the Assyrian period.
|- style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD" | Hatra
|
| IrqNineveh Governorate,
| Cultural:IrqHat(ii)(iii)(iv)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1985
| The fortified Parthian city of Hatra withstood repeated attacks by the Roman Empire in the 2nd century. Its architecture reflects both Hellenistic and Roman influences.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Assur
|
| IrqSaladin Governorate,
| Cultural:IrqAsh(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2003
| Located on the Tigris and dating from the 3rd millennium BCE, Ashur was the first capital of the Assyrian Empire and the religious centre of the Assyrians. Following its destruction by the Babylonians, the city was briefly revived during the Parthian period.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Samarra
|
| IrqSaladin Governorate,
| Cultural:IrqSam(ii)(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2007
| Located on the Tigris, the Islamic city of Samarra was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. It contains two of the largest mosques and several of the largest palaces in the Islamic world, in addition to being among the finest example of Abbasid-era town-planning.
|-
! As-Salt
|
| JorBalqa Governorate,
| Cultural: (ii)(iii)
| 24.68 (61.0)
| 2021
| Established on three closely-spaced hills in the Balqa (region), As-Salt was the main settlement on the East Bank of the Jordan River that served as a cultural, commercial and financial hub. This prosperity allowed for the influx of people from the region who settled in As-Salt, creating a distinct city built with yellow limestone that had European Art Nouveau and Neo-Colonial styles combined with local traditions.
|-
! scope="row" | Al-Maghtas
|
| Jor
| Cultural:JorBap(iii)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 2015

|-
! scope="row" | Petra
|
| JorMa'an Governorate,
| Cultural:JorPet(i)(iii)(iv)
| 26,171 (64670)
| align="center" | 1985
| The Nabataean city of Petra was a major trading hub between Arabia, Egypt and Syria-Phoenicia, famed for its rock-cut architecture as well as its mining and water engineering systems.
|-

|
| JorZarqa Governorate,
| Cultural:JorQus(i)(iii)(iv)
| 0.0445 (0.101)
| align="center" | 1985
| The desert castle of Quseir Amra was built in the early 8th century, and had served both as a fortress and an Umayyad royal palace. The site also noted for its extensive frescoes, constituting an important and unique example of early Islamic art.
|-
! scope="row" | Um ar-Rasas
|
| JorMadaba Governorate,
| Cultural:JorUme(i)(iv)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 2005
| Established as a Roman military camp, Um er-Rasas grew into a settlement by the 5th century, inhabited successively by Christian and Islamic communities. The largely unexcavated site contains ruins of Roman fortifications, churches with well-preserved mosaic floors and two stylite towers.
|-
! scope="row" | Wadi Rum
|
| Jor
| Mixed:JorWad(iii)(v)(vii)
|
| align="center" | 2005
| Situated in southern Jordan, Wadi Rum features a great variety of desert landforms including sandstone valleys, natural arches, gorges, cliffs, landslides and caverns. |-
! scope="row" | Anjar
|
| LbnBeqaa Governorate,
| Cultural:LbnAnj(iii)(iv)
| —
| align="center" | 1984
| Established in the early 8th century, the city of Anjar was quickly abandoned following the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate, leaving behind ruins of walls, towers, palaces, mosques and baths, constituting an example of Umayyad period town-planning.
|-
! scope="row" | Baalbek
|
| LbnBaalbek-Hermel Governorate,
| Cultural:LbnBal(i)(iv)
| —
| align="center" | 1984
| Previously known as Heliopolis, the Phoenician city of Baalbek hosts some of the largest and best preserved Roman temples, including the Temples of Jupiter, Venus and Bacchus.
|-
! scope="row" | Byblos
|
| LbnMount Lebanon Governorate,
| Cultural:LbnByb(iii)(iv)(vi)
| —
| align="center" | 1984
| Continuously inhabited since the Neolithic Era, Byblos was one of the oldest cities of Phoenician origin. It has since witnessed Persian, Roman, Crusader and Ottoman occupation, each exerting influence upon its architecture. Byblos also played a significant role in the diffusion of the Phoenician alphabet.
|-
! scope="row" | Kadisha Valley
|
| LbnNorth Lebanon Governorate,
| Cultural:LbnOua(iii)(iv)
| —
| align="center" | 1998

The Forest of the Cedars of God is among the last locations where Cedrus libani still grows, historically one of the most prized construction materials.
|-
! scope="row" | Rachid Karami International Fair-Tripoli
|
| LbnNorth Lebanon Governorate,
| Cultural:LbnOua(ii)(iv)
| —
| align="center" | 2022
|Located in northern Lebanon, the Rachid Karameh International Fair of Tripoli was designed in 1962 by the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer on a 70-hectare site located between the historic centre of Tripoli and the Al Mina port. The fair was the flagship project of Lebanon's modernization policy in the 1960s.
|-
! scope="row" | Tyre
|
| LbnSouth Lebanon Governorate,
| Cultural:LbnTyr(iii)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1984
| The ancient Phoenician city of Tyre was one of the foremost maritime powers in the eastern Mediterranean and reportedly where purple dye was discovered. Extant archaeological remains mainly date back to Roman times, including baths, an arena, a colonnaded road, a triumphal arch, an aqueduct and a hippodrome.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Cyrene
|
| LibJabal al Akhdar,
| Cultural:LibArcCyr(ii)(iii)(vi)
| —
| align="center" | 1982
| The formerly Greek colony of Cyrene was Romanized and transformed into a capital, until it was destroyed by the 365 Crete earthquake. The thousand-year-old ruins have remained renowned since the 18th century.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Leptis Magna
|
| LibKhoms,
| Cultural:LibArcLep(i)(ii)(iii)
| —
| align="center" | 1982
| The Roman city of Leptis Magna was enlarged by Emperor Septimius Severus, who was born there. Public monuments, a harbour, a marketplace, storehouses, shops, and homes were among the reasons for its induction into the list.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Sabratha
|
| LibZawiya District,
| Cultural:LibArcSab(iii)
| —
| align="center" | 1982
| Founded as a Phoenician trading post, Sabratha was briefly ruled by Masinissa of Numidia before its Romanization and reconstruction in the 2nd and 3rd centuries.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Ghadamès
|
| LibNalut District,
| Cultural:LibOld(v)
| —
| align="center" | 1986
| Located in an oasis, Ghadames is among the oldest of pre-Saharan cities and represents a traditional domestic architecture with vertical division of functions.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Acacus Mountains
|
| LibFezzan,
| Cultural:LibRoc(iii)
| —
| align="center" | 1985
| The massif of Tadrart Acacus contains thousands of cave paintings in different styles, dating from 12,000 BCE to 100 CE, reflecting changes of flora and fauna in the region as well as different lifestyles of successive populations in the Sahara.
|-
! scope="row" | Ancient Ksour of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata
|
| MauritaniaOuadane,Chinguetti,Tichitt,and Oualata,
| Cultural:MauAnc(iii)(iv)(v)
| —
| align="center" | 1996
| These four settlements were founded in the 11th and 12th centuries, originally meant to serve caravan trade routes across the Sahara. They gradually evolved into Islamic cultural centres, bearing witness to the nomadic lifestyle of the populations of western Sahara.
|-
! scope="row" | Banc d'Arguin National Park
|
| MauritaniaNouadhibou and Azefal,
| Natural:MauBan(ix)(x)
|
| align="center" | 1989
| The park consists of sand dunes, coastal swamps, small islands, and shallow bodies of water; all bordering the coast of the Atlantic Ocean. Birds are often found to migrate in the area, accompanied by various species of sea turtles and dolphins, whose presence fishermen often use to attract fish.
|-
! scope="row" | Volubilis
|
| MorFès-Meknès,
| Cultural:MorArcVol(ii)(iii)(iv)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1997
| The important Roman outpost of Volubilis was founded in the 3rd century BCE as the capital of Mauretania, later becoming the capital of the Idrisid dynasty. It contained many buildings, the remains of which have survived extensively to this day.
|-
! scope="row" | Meknes
|
| MorFès-Meknès,
| Cultural:MorHis(iv)
| —
| align="center" | 1996
| The former capital of the Alaouite dynasty was founded in the 11th century by the Almoravids and turned into a city with Spanish-Moorish influence during the 17th and 18th centuries.
|-
! scope="row" | Aït Benhaddou
|
| MorDrâa-Tafilalet,
| Cultural:MorKsa(iv)(v)
|
| align="center" | 1987
| The Ksar of Ait-Ben-Haddou is an example of a traditional pre-Saharan habitat in southern Morocco, surrounded by high walls and reinforced with corner towers.
|-
! scope="row" | Essaouira
|
| MorMarrakesh-Safi,
| Cultural:MorEss(ii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2001
| Built during the late 18th century, the fortified seaport of Essaouira has a mix of North African and European architecture, and was a major trading hub between the Sahara and Europe.
|-
! scope="row" | Fes el Bali
|
| MorFez,
| Cultural:MorMedinaofFez(ii)(v)
|
| align="center" | 1981
| Fez was founded in the 9th century and reached its apogee as the capital of the Marinid dynasty in the 13th and 14th centuries, from which its urban fabric and major monuments date. It also hosts the world's oldest university, the University of Al Quaraouiyine.
|-
! scope="row" | Marrakesh
|
| MorMarrakesh-Safi,
| Cultural:MorMedinaofMarra(i)(ii)(iv)(v)
|
| align="center" | 1985
| Marrakesh was founded in the 1070s and remained a political, economic, and cultural centre for a long time. Monuments from that period include the Koutoubia Mosque, the kasbah, and the battlements. The city also holds newer features, including palaces and madrasas.
|-
! scope="row" | Tétouan
|
| MorTanger-Tetouan-Al Hoceima,
| Cultural:MorMedinaofTet(ii)(iv)(v)
|
| align="center" | 1997
| Morocco's most complete medina at Tétouan served as the main point of contact between Morocco and Andalusia during the 8th century. The town was rebuilt by Andalusian refugees following the Reconquista, the influence of which is evident in its art and architecture.
|-
! scope="row" | Rabat
|
| MorRabat,
| Cultural:MorRab(ii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2012
| Rebuilt under the direction of the French from 1912 to the 1930s, Rabat blends historic and modern features, such as botanical gardens, the Hassan Mosque, and the remnants of Moorish and Andalusian settlements from the 17th century.
|-
! scope="row" | El Jadida
|
| MorCasablanca-Settat,
| Cultural:MorPor(ii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2004
| The Portuguese fortification of Mazagan, akin to early Renaissance military design from the early 16th century, was taken over by Morocco in 1769. Surviving buildings include the cistern and a Gothic church.
|-
! scope="row" | Aflaj Irrigation Systems of Oman
|
| OmnDakhiliyah, Sharqiyah and Batinah Regions,
| Cultural:OmnAfl(v)
|
| align="center" | 2006
| The five Aflaj systems inscribed represents an irrigation method dating back to at least 500 CE. Such system effectively distribute water through gravity, as it flows to support agricultural and domestic use.
|-
! scope="row" | Qalhat
|
| OmnAsh Sharqiyah South Governorate,
| Cultural:OmnQal(ii)(iii)
|
| align="center" | 2018
|
|-
! scope="row" | Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn
|
| OmnAd Dhahirah Region,
| Cultural:OmnArc(iii)(iv)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 1988
| Located in the interior of the Sultanate, Bat, al-Khutm and al-Ayn are among the best preserved ensembles of settlements and necropolises from the 3rd millennium BCE in Eastern Arabia and the world. The necropolis of Bat, in particular, reflects the funeral practices of the Early Bronze Age in Oman.
|-
! scope="row" | Bahla Fort
|
| OmnAd Dakhiliyah Region,
| Cultural:OmnBah(iv)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 1987
| The fort is part of Bahla, an oasis settlement and formerly the capital of the Nabhani dynasty, who dominated Oman and prospered in the Arabian Peninsula during the Late Middle Ages.
|-
! scope="row" | Land of Frankincense
|
| OmnDhofar Governorate,
| Cultural:OmnLan(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2000
| The ancient ports of Khor Rori and Al-Baleed, the caravan oasis of Shisr and Wadi Dawkah in southern Arabia were crucial in the production and distribution of frankincense, one of the most sought-after items of luxury in Antiquity.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Old City of Jerusalem
|
| JerEast Jerusalem
| Cultural:JerOld(ii)(iii)(vi)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 1981
| A holy city for three of the world's major religions, Jerusalem contains more than 200 historic monuments, including the Dome of the Rock, the Wailing Wall and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
|-

|
| PalBethlehem Governorate,
| Cultural:PalBir(ii)(iii)
|
| align="center" | 2012
| The site is traditionally identified as the birthplace of Jesus. The church, built in the 4th century and reconstructed in the 6th century, holds prominent religious significance to both Christians and Muslims.
|-
|
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Battir
|
| PalBethlehem Governorate,
| Cultural:PalPal(iv)(v)
|
| align="center" | 2014
| The hill landscape of Battir features stone terraces for market garden, grapevine and olive production, supported by a traditional irrigation system.
|-
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Hebron
|
| PalHebron Governorate,
| Cultural:PalPal (ii)(iv)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 2017
| The centre of interest of the town was the site of Al-Ibrahimi Mosque/The tomb of the Patriarchs whose buildings are in a compound built in the 1st century CE to protect the tombs of the patriarch Abraham / Ibrahim and his family.

| align="center" | 2018
|

| Located on the coast of the Red Sea, Jeddah grew into a major commercial centre in the 7th century, and has long served as the principal gateway for pilgrims to Mecca.
|-
! scope="row" | Rock Art in the Ha'il Region
|
| SauHa'il Region,
| Cultural:SauRoc(i)(iii)
|
| align="center" | 2015
| The sites of Jabel Umm Sinman and Jabal al-Manjor and Raat contain a large number of petroglyphs and inscriptions, covering 10,000 years of human history.
|-
! scope="row" | ‘Uruq Bani Mu’arid
|
| SauNajran,
| Natural:SauRoc(vii)(ix)
|
| align="center" | 2023
| The property encompasses the western part of the greatest expanse of windblown sand on Earth, known as Ar Rub' al-KhaIi, and conserves one of the Earth’s most spectacular desert landscapes.
|-
! scope="row" | Qaryat al-Faw
|
| SauRiyadh Province,
| Cultural:SauHis(ii)(v)
|
| align="center" | 2024
| Lying at a strategic point of the ancient trade routes of the Arabian Peninsula, the property was abruptly abandoned around the 5th century CE.
|-
! scope="row" | Meroë
|
| SdnRiver Nile State,
| Cultural:SdnArc(ii)(iii)(iv)(v)
|
| align="center" | 2011
| Meroe was the centre of the Kingdom of Kush, a major force active from the 8th century BCE to the 4th century CE. It is home to pyramids, temples, and domestic buildings, among other vestiges.
|-
! scope="row" | Jebel Barkal
|
| SdnNorthern State,
| Cultural:SdnGeb(i)(ii)(iii)(iv)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 2003
| The archaeological sites of Gebel Barkal, Kurru, Nuri, Sanam and Zuma in the Nile Valley testify to the Napatan and Meroitic civilisations. They host a series of pyramids, tombs, temples, palaces, burial mounds and funerary chambers.
|-
! scope="row" | Sanganeb Marine National Park and Dungonab Bay
|
| Sdn
| Natural:SdnSan(vii)(ix)(x)
|
| align="center" | 2016
| Situated in the central Red Sea, Sanganeb, Dungonab Bay and Mukkawar Island feature a diverse system of coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, beaches and islets, and host populations of seabirds, marine mammals, fish, sharks, turtles, manta rays and dugongs.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Ancient Aleppo
|
| SyrAleppo Governorate,
| Cultural:SyrAncAle(iii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 1986
| Situated at the crossroads of several trade routes, Aleppo has been successively ruled, among others, by the Romans, Ayyubids, Mameluks and Ottomans, each leaving significant influence in its architectural fabric, resulting in a diverse cityscape. Major structures include the Citadel, the Great Mosque and the Madrasa Halawiye.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Ancient City of Bosra
|
| SyrDaraa Governorate,
| Cultural:SyrAncBos(i)(iii)(vi)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 1980
| Formerly a Nabataean settlement, Bosra was conquered by the Romans in the 2nd century CE and made capital of Arabia. It came under Islamic rule in the 7th century. Remains of the ancient city include a theatre, a basilica, a cathedral, a mosque and a madrasa, among others.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Old city of Damascus
|
| SyrDamascus Governorate,
| Cultural:SyrAncDam(i)(ii)(iii)(iv)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| Established the 3rd millennium BCE, Damascus is considered to be one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. As the capital of the Umayyads, it has been of significant influence to the Arab world. The Great Mosque is among the largest in the world and the oldest sites of continuous prayer since the beginnings of Islam.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Dead Cities
|
| Syr
| Cultural:SyrAncVil(iii)(iv)(v)
|
| align="center" | 2011
| The site comprises some 40 villages, dating from the 1st to 7th centuries and abandoned in the 8th to 10th centuries. They provide an insight into rural life in Late Antiquity and during the Byzantine period.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Krac des Chevaliers and Sahyun Castle
|
| SyrHoms and Latakia Governorates,
| Cultural:SyrCra(ii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 2006
| The Crac des Chevaliers and the Qal'at Salah El-Din are regarded as two of the most prominent examples of castles during the Crusader period, demonstrating an evolution of fortifications and exchange of influences in defensive technology.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Palmyra
|
| SyrHoms Governorate,
| Cultural:SyrSit(i)(ii)(iv)
|
| align="center" | 1980
| Palmyra came under Roman rule in the 1st century CE, and grew to become one of the most important cultural centres of the ancient world. Its extensive ruins include remains of the Great Colonnade, the Temple of Bel, the Camp of Diocletian and the Roman Theatre.
|-
! scope="row" | Carthage
|
| TunTunis Governorate,
| Cultural:TunArc(ii)(iii)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| Founded in the 9th century BCE, Carthage developed into a trading empire spanning the Mediterranean. The city was destroyed in 146 BCE in the Punic Wars at the hands of the Romans, but was later reestablished.
|-
! scope="row" | Dougga
|
| TunBeBéja Governorate,
| Cultural:TunDou(ii)(iii)
|
| align="center" | 1997
| The site features the ruins of Dougga, a former capital of a Libyan–Punic state, which flourished under the Romans and the Byzantines, but went into decline in the Islamic period.
|-
! scope="row" | Amphitheatre of El Jem
|
| TunMahdia Governorate,
| Cultural:TunEld(iv)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| Built during the 3rd century, the Amphitheatre of El Jem is North Africa's largest amphitheatre, and the largest one built outside of Italy, with a capacity of 35,000 spectators, regarded as among the most accomplished examples of Roman architecture of its kind.
|-
! scope="row" | Lake Ichkeul
|
| TunBiBizerte Governorate,
| Natural:TunIch(x)
|
| align="center" | 1980
| Ichkeul Lake and the surrounding wetlands is a destination for hundreds of thousands of migrating birds, including ducks, geese, storks and pink flamingos. It was once part of a chain that extended across North Africa.
|-
! scope="row" | Kairouan
|
| TunKairouan Governorate,
| Cultural:TunKai(i)(ii)(iii)(v)(vi)
|
| align="center" | 1988
| Founded in 670, Kairouan was the former capital of Ifriqiya and flourished in the 9th century. Its heritage includes the Mosque of Uqba and the Mosque of the Three Gates.
|-
! scope="row" | Medina of Sousse
|
| TunSousse Governorate,
| Cultural:TunMedinaofSou(iii)(iv)(v)
|
| align="center" | 1988
| A prime example of a town from the early Islamic period, Sousse was an important commercial and military port during the 9th century.
|-
! scope="row" | Medina of Tunis
|
| TunTunis Governorate,
| Cultural:TunMedinaofTun(ii)(iii)(v)
|
| align="center" | 1979
| The Medina of Tunis contains some 700 monuments, including palaces, mosques, mausoleums, madrasah and fourtains, testifying to Tunis' golden age from the 12th to the 16th century.
|-
! scope="row" | Kerkouane
|
| TunNabeul Governorate,
| Cultural:TunPun(iii)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 1985
| Abandoned in 250 BCE during the First Punic War and never rebuilt, Kerkuane is the only surviving example of a Phoenicio–Punic settlement.
|-
! scope="row" | Al Ain
|
| UaeAbu Dhabi,
| Cultural:UaeCul(iii)(iv)(v)
|
| align="center" | 2011
| Situated in a desert region, Al Ain has been occupied since the Neolithic period, hosting stone tombs from the 3rd millennium BCE, wells, adobe constructions and one of the oldest examples of the aflaj irrigation system at Bidaa Bint Saud.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Zabid
|
| YemAl Hudaydah Governorate,
| Cultural:YemHis(iii)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 1993
| Zabid was the capital of Yemen from the 13th to the 15th century. Its Islamic university greatly contributed to the spread of Islamic knowledge.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Sanaa
|
| YemSana'a Governorate,
| Cultural:YemOldSan(iv)(v)(vi)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 1986
| Situated in a mountain valley, Sana'a has been continuously inhabited for more than 2,500 years. It became a centre for the spread of Islam in the 7th and 8th centuries. The city is home to the unique rammed-earth tower-houses, in addition to 103 mosques and 14 hammams built before the 11th century.
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Shibam
|
| YemHadhramaut Governorate,
| Cultural:YemOldShi(iii)(iv)(v)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 1982
| The 16th-century walled city of Shibam is among the oldest and best examples of vertical urban planning, with its distinct mud brick tower houses garnering it the nickname "the Manhattan of the desert".
|-style="background-color:#FFE6BD"
! scope="row" style="background-color: #FFE6BD"| Landmarks of the Ancient Kingdom of Saba, Marib
|
| YemMarib Governorate,
| Cultural:Marib(iii)(iv)
| align="center" | —
| align="center" | 2023
| Marib was the center of the Ancient Kingdom of Saba. It consists of seven archaeological sites; Barran Temple, the Awam Temple (pictured), the ancient city of Marib, Old Marib Dam, and the ancient city of Sirwah.
|-
! scope="row" | Socotra
|
| YemSocotra Governorate,
| Natural:YemSoc(x)
|
| align="center" | 2008
| Although part of the African landmass, the Socotra Archipelago is administered from Yemen. It is known for its great biodiversity and distinct flora and fauna, with a large number of endemic species found nowhere else on earth. It also supports a broad range of avian and marine life.

! scope="row" | The forts of Rostaq and al-Hazm
|
| Al Batinah South
| 1998
| (cultural)
| Located in a large oasis, the fort at Rustaq dates to the preislamic period when it was an important market place. Later additions include four towers and outer walls (pictured). There are several ancient houses remaining, as well as a funerary mosque. The Al Hazm Castle dates to the 18th century. It was built under the Yaruba dynasty. It is a rectangular two-storey structure with a narrow inner courtyard.
|-
! scope="row" | Al Hallaniyyat Islands Proposed Nature Reserve
|
| Dhofar
| 2013
| x (natural)
| The islands are barren with sparse Tamarix and Acacia trees. The surrounding sea is rich in corals and is home to numerous fish species, as well as dolphins and whales. The sandy beaches are important grounds for loggerhead sea turtles and green turtles to lay their eggs. There are numerous bird species, such as the masked booby, Audubon's shearwater, and red-billed tropicbird nesting on the islands as there are no predators.
|-
! scope="row" | Bar al Hakman Proposed Nature Reserve
|
| Al Wusta
| 2013
| x (natural)
| Bar al Hakman peninsula has sandy dunes, mudflats, mangrove forests, and marine habitats with seagrass meadows and coral reefs. The area is important for migratory birds that gather here in winter in large numbers, with 140 species reported. It is also important for sea turtles that lay their eggs here.
|-
! scope="row" | Smahan's Mountain Nature Reserve
|
| Dhofar
| 2013
| vii, x (natural)
| The reserve is the largest protected area in the country. The rugged terrain comprises plateaus, canyons, wadis, and escarpments. The area is home to the critically endangered Arabian leopard and Dhofar shrew, as well as the Nubian ibex, Arabian gazelle, and caracal.
|-
! scope="row" | al Dimaniyyat Islands Nature Reserve
|
| Muscat
| 2013
| x (natural)
| The islands are important for hawksbill sea turtles and green turtles that lay their eggs there. There are numerous bird species, such as the red-billed tropicbird and different species of terns nesting on the islands. The surrounding sea is home to corals, sea snakes, three species of dolphins, and humpback whales.
|-
! scope="row" | Ras al Had Turtle Reserve and the Heritage Site of Ras al Jinz
|
| Ash Sharqiyah South
| 2013
| ii, iii, x (mixed)
| The reserve extends  along the coast and comprises sandy and rocky beaches, two lagoons, and mangrove bushes. The beaches are important nesting grounds for green turtles, with thousands visiting every year to lay their eggs. There are also archaeological remains in the reserve, with graves and settlements from the early Holocene to the Iron Age. Finds include objects that originated in Bronze Age India.
|-
! scope="row" | Cultural Landscape of Bisya & Salut and its Archaeological Remains
|
| Ad Dakhiliyah
| 2014
| ii, iii, iv, v, vi (cultural)
| The area, located at a meeting point of two wadis, has several archaeological sites from Bronze and Iron Age. There are remains of settlements form as early as the 4th millennium BCE when people practiced agriculture, made possible by irrigation. There are also monuments and numerous tombs from different periods. The material remains indicate people traded with the civilizations of Mesopotamia, Iran, and Indus Valley.
